transcript:
MEETING HEADER:
Date: 2026-12-09 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ravi (Brightshore Head of Platform), Lena (Brightshore Sr Cloud Eng), Sam (Brightshore Security)
Shared artifacts: Redwood private deployment overview deck (link), network intake spreadsheet (link), SOC2 summary (to be shared)

AUTO-SUMMARY (auto): customer wants private onramp; main blockers are egress IPs, region gating for customer data, and KMS/HSM integration.

00:00:05 - Maya: Okay everybody thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on this. we also have diego and priya from the se team. can i get a quick intro from your side?
00:00:24 - Ravi: Yep, hi, i'm ravi, head of platform at brightshore. we own infra and platform for trading and compliance services. we want LLM features but all data must stay in EU regions, and most workloads on private network.
00:00:40 - Lena: lena here, i'll be doing the nitty gritty, network, subnets, we have transit gateway and a pair of VPCs per region.
00:00:48 - Sam: sam, security architect, my main questions are around key management and audit logs plus how we control egress IPs.

00:01:10 - Maya: great. quick agenda — we want to understand your topology, gating constraints, timeline and what success looks like. then diego will walk through options: private endpoints, peering, transit gateway patterns and fallback with dedicated capacity.

00:02:02 - Diego: cool. high level — Redwood Private can be deployed with private endpoints (privatelink-style), cross-account VPC peering, or via a transit gw depending on scale. each has tradeoffs on scaling, ip management, and egress. 

00:02:35 - Lena: when you say private endpoints, do you mean AWS privatelink or your managed private endpoint? we run AWS and GCP, prefer not to open public egress.
00:02:47 - Diego: yeah we support native cloud privatelink endpoints in AWS and equivalent in GCP (private service connect), and we also have an option for cross-account peering if you want full L3 connectivity. for higher scale transit gw is common.

00:03:20 - Ravi: our compliance team wants a pinned set of egress IPs so we can put them into our approved list. how static are your egress IPs for private deployments?
00:03:35 - Priya: short answer — we can provide a range per deployment; for Dedicated we provide fixed NAT egress IPs, for Private there's an option to route through customer NAT (so egress IP is yours) or use Redwood-managed egress with assigned IP blocks. depends on architecture.

00:04:12 - Sam: if you route through customer NAT that means traffic to the model runtime stays within our VPC and you call back over private link? i'm worried about KV cache or telemetry leaving our network.
00:04:29 - Diego: good point. our runtime sits in the deployment in your VPC for Private — so inference dataplane can be entirely in your network. control plane still talks to Redwood for management, but that's via private connectivity to our control plane (private peering/VPN) if you choose. KV cache is local to the runtime instance.

00:05:05 - Ravi: okay — so control plane still needs some connectivity, is that over internet or can you do private VPN to your control plane?
00:05:16 - Maya: we offer a private control plane option: a customer-managed control plane connector over IPSec VPN or AWS Direct Connect/PrivateLink into our control plane. for highly regulated customers we do a VPC-to-VPC peering + restricted management endpoint approach.

00:05:48 - Lena: latency is key — trading models want sub-50ms for inference at 512 tokens. can private routing meet that?
00:06:00 - Diego: depends on region proximity & instance type. if you run the runtime in your same region with dedicated GPUs, sub-50ms tail is achievable. we usually recommend colocating runtime in the same AZs as your services and using local private endpoints to minimize round trip.

00:06:38 - Sam: for KMS — we need encryption keys to remain in our KMS/HSM; can Redwood integrate with a customer KMS?
00:06:52 - Priya: yes, we support customer-managed KMS in Private. we can integrate with AWS KMS (with grants) or external HSM via KMIP in some on-prem scenarios. logs can be shipped to your CloudWatch/Stackdriver/Splunk; audit events are available from the runtime. we'll share the exact integration doc.

00:07:25 - Ravi: region gating — we have EU-only data residency; can Redwood guarantee that data never leaves region X?
00:07:39 - Diego: Redwood Private can be deployed entirely in EU regions; control plane endpoints we can localize for enterprise customers, otherwise management meta flows might need dedicated regional hosting. we can commit to not replicate customer data to other regions as part of the contract — need legal SLA for that.

00:08:10 - Lena: what's the typical network setup you see for customers with multiple accounts and strict ACLs?
00:08:20 - Diego: commonly: per-region VPCs with peering or transit gw back to a central services VPC. Redwood runtime lives in a service VPC that you own; we operate via an IAM-role cross-account model, or we can use privatelink endpoints into your account. If you use privatelink, only the service endpoint is exposed, no full mesh.

00:09:01 - Ravi: any gotchas around NACLs/security groups for privatelink? we have restrictive NACLs.
00:09:10 - Priya: privatelink requires opening the endpoint and NAT to allow flows; security groups on the ENIs must permit the control traffic ports — we'll provide a checklist of ports and protocols. sometimes customers forget ephemeral port ranges for streaming APIs.

00:09:45 - Sam: certification wise do you have SOC2 and ISO docs? we need to show audit artifacts to auditors.
00:09:53 - Maya: yes SOC2 is public, we'll send a SOC2 summary and our security whitepaper. for Private deployments we also produce a deployment-specific attestation.

00:10:12 - Lena: you mentioned fallback to Dedicated — how does that work if our Private runs out of capacity? we can't have data cross borders.
00:10:24 - Diego: automatic fallback by default goes to a compatible model variant in the same region if available. fallback to Redwood-hosted Shared or Dedicated would require data egress agreement; we can configure strict no-fallback policy if you require absolute containment.

00:11:02 - Ravi: timeline — we're aiming for pilot in Q1, should be quick but need legal sign-off. what do you need from us to scope pilot?
00:11:13 - Maya: we'll need your preferred regions, target QPS, model choices, list of endpoints that need private access, and your network contacts for runbook. diego will produce a pilot network diagram.

00:11:40 - Lisa (interruption from Oliver): sorry — oliver here, question on egress logging. can logs be collected before they leave the VPC? we want full request traces in our SIEM without sending PII to a third party.
00:11:55 - Priya: yes audit logs and request traces can be forwarded directly to your SIEM via logs agent or S3 bucket in your account. we can filter telemetry and redact PII on the runtime.

00:12:30 - Diego: quick note on scale: if you have heavy concurrency we recommend dedicated GPU pools and autoscaling; that affects IP footprint and subnet planning as pods spin up. so planning ephemeral IP ranges matters for firewall rules.

00:12:58 - Ravi: what about NAT gateways per AZ vs centralized NAT? cost tradeoff?
00:13:08 - Diego: centralized NAT is cheaper but increases egress blast radius and potential single point; per-AZ NAT increases cost but reduces latency and isolates faults. We'll model both options in the network intake doc.

00:13:45 - Sam: encryption of logs in transit and at rest — you said we can use our KMS, what about attestation that keys are never exfiltrated?
00:13:55 - Priya: keys remain in your KMS and we never export raw key material; encryption is performed with grants and we can produce key usage logs as part of audit evidence. we'll include the KMS integration flow in the docs.

00:14:30 - Maya: ok i'm going to open the architecture whiteboard — diego, can you run through two proposed topologies: (A) privatelink endpoints with customer-managed NAT and (B) transit gw + cross-account runtime?

00:14:48 - Diego: sure. Topology A: service endpoints via private link — minimal L3 footprint, you control egress via your NAT. Pros: easiest to satisfy egress ip control and data residency. Cons: scaling many endpoints across many regions can become operationally heavier. Topology B: transit gateway with cross-account runtime — easier to scale, single peering, but you need to manage routing and possibly accept egress IPs owned by the runtime unless routed through your NAT.

00:15:35 - Lena: with privatelink do we still need to open outbound to your control plane?
00:15:42 - Diego: control plane calls can be made over a separate management connection — we can use a VPN or direct connect; or we can publish a management endpoint into your VPC using privatelink. we'll recommend the privatelink for control plane to keep everything private.

00:16:10 - Ravi: any constraints around IP ranges? we have limited RFC1918 space per account.
00:16:19 - Priya: we typically ask for /20 or /21 depending on scale; if space is tight we can use shared subnets in a centrally managed services VPC and cross-account IAM roles to minimize additional ranges. we'll capture this in intake.

00:16:44 - Sam: compliance question — do you provide per-request audit logs including model version and prompt hash and can we retain them for 7 years?
00:16:56 - Diego: we can produce per-request audit metadata (not raw prompts unless requested), model version, timestamps, and hashes. retention duration is configurable; longer retention may require additional storage and cost. we can integrate with your archival policies.

00:17:30 - Maya: quick check on stakeholders — ravi, who's the signer for legal?
00:17:36 - Ravi: our procurement head, emily, will handle contracts; legal has a special team for data residency clauses.

00:17:50 - Lena: one more nuance: we use strict egress filtering at our firewall and only allow specific destination IPs. if you provide a list of IPs that can be whitelisted that will unblock the network team.
00:18:03 - Maya: we'll provide an IP range list per proposed topology. for privatelink you only need endpoints and internal ENIs; for transit gw we'll provide egress ranges if we manage NAT.

00:18:30 - Ravi: what about cost visibility — if we choose Private with dedicated pools how do we see token-level costs?
00:18:40 - Diego: Redwood Console provides token and per-request latency/cost breakdown even for Private; we also offer billing export to your billing system and per-route metrics. cost for dedicated pools is a reserved capacity model plus usage.

00:19:10 - Sam: security posture — SSO and RBAC integration?
00:19:18 - Priya: we support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC at org/team/token level. for Private we can integrate to your IdP for the console and runtime admin APIs.

00:19:45 - Oliver: question on upgrades/rollouts — how do we handle model upgrades without downtime?
00:19:53 - Diego: we support canary rollouts with routing policies and automatic fallback. rollouts happen within your VPC for Private so the traffic never leaves your network.

00:20:20 - Ravi: okay sounds good. can you outline the pilot acceptance criteria?
00:20:28 - Maya: sure — basic list: 1) runtime deployed in EU region, 2) private endpoint reachable from your app VPC with TLS and auth, 3) egress IPs validated with firewall rules, 4) KMS integration validated for model artifact encryption, 5) latency under target for a representative workload. does that align?
00:20:52 - Ravi: yes that's perfect.

00:21:10 - Sam: any blockers we should know now? like cross-account IAM permissions or special ACLs?
00:21:18 - Diego: usually we need: cross-account role creation, endpoint service acceptance or peering approval, security group rules for the runtime, and explicit NAT planning. also sometimes customers have strict proxy egress which requires allowlisting management endpoints.

00:21:45 - Lena: timeline on docs?
00:21:50 - Maya: i'll share SOC2 and the security whitepaper tonight; Diego will push the network intake doc and sample diagrams by monday.

00:22:05 - Ravi: good. on legal/regulatory — we'll need a clause about no data replication outside EU unless we approve. can that be accommodated?
00:22:15 - Maya: yes we can draft region-locking language for the MSA; will loop in contracts after the technical fit.

00:22:36 - (short side conversation)
00:23:05 - Diego: anything else on network egress?
00:23:08 - Oliver: if we go transit gw + your managed nat what's the expected egress ip churn?
00:23:16 - Priya: minimal — for dedicated pools we minimize churn and we can reserve static egress blocks; for dynamic autoscaling there is some ephemeral churn but within a predictable cidr. we'll provide guidance.

00:23:45 - Maya: ok let's recap next steps and owners. diego will produce two network diagrams and checklist, maya will share security docs, ravi will get IP allowlist and desired regions. we'll schedule follow-up deep dive with networking and security.

00:24:10 - Ravi: can we do the follow-up next tuesday morning?
00:24:18 - Maya: yes i'll send calendar invite for Tues 2026-12-15 09:00 CET unless that conflicts.

00:24:30 - Sam: i'll invite our compliance lead so legal questions can be handled live.

00:24:45 - Maya: perfect. any final questions?
00:24:50 - Lena: just one — for privatelink, what's the expected time to establish endpoints once we accept the service?
00:24:58 - Diego: typically 1-2 hours for endpoint creation and acceptance, and then validation; overall network validation can take a day depending on approvals.

00:25:20 - Ravi: great thanks everyone.
00:25:24 - Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with docs and invite.

(end of recorded transcript — remaining ~23 minutes were Q/A and whiteboarding noted in meeting notes, summarised above)

NOTES: There were a few transcription artifacts where product names showed differently (e.g., privatelink referred as private link and sometimes as private endpoint). The team requested explicit IP ranges, region lock language, SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
